title: Given a list of words, find the longest word that can be built one character at a time, where every prefix of that word is also present in the list; break ties by taking the smallest word in dictionary order. Explain how the Trie pattern solves it, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Longest Word in Dictionary (Longest Word Buildable One Character at a Time)
keyPoints: A word is buildable one character at a time if every prefix of that word is also a word in the list.
Insert all words into a trie, marking each word's end node.
DFS from the root, only descending through nodes marked as complete words.
Track the longest reachable word, breaking ties by lexicographic (dictionary) order.
Visiting children in sorted character order gives the lexicographic tie-break for free.
Time is O(total characters) for trie construction and traversal.
This is a traversal application of the Trie pattern, not a search application.

s1_definition.oneliner: Only descend through trie nodes that are themselves complete words, and keep the longest reachable path.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Longest buildable word** – finds the longest word from a list where every prefix of that word is also a word in the list.
- **Trie construction** – insert all words into a trie, marking each word's end node.
- **Word-only DFS** – traverse the trie from the root, only stepping into children that are marked as complete words.
- **Tie-breaking** – among words of equal length, the lexicographically smallest wins; visiting children in sorted order handles this.
- **Complexity** – O(sum of all word lengths) for both construction and traversal.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India builds product feature codes incrementally, where each longer code must extend a code that already exists. Rajesh wants the longest code reachable by adding one character at a time, with every intermediate code being a valid registered code.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
Trie for words: ["a", "ap", "app", "appl", "apple", "b", "ba", "bat"]

            root
           /    \
          a[w]   b[w]
          |      |
         p[w]   a[w]
          |      |
         p[w]   t[w]
          |
         l[w]
          |
         e[w] = "apple"

  [w] = marked as a complete word

  DFS (word-only descent):
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ root -> 'a' (word) -> descend            │
  │   'a' -> 'p' (word) -> descend           │
  │     'ap' -> 'p' (word) -> descend        │
  │       'app' -> 'l' (word) -> descend     │
  │         'appl' -> 'e' (word) -> descend  │
  │           'apple' -> no more children    │
  │           best = "apple" (length 5)      │
  │                                          │
  │ root -> 'b' (word) -> descend            │
  │   'b' -> 'a' (word) -> descend           │
  │     'ba' -> 't' (word) -> descend        │
  │       'bat' -> no more children          │
  │       "bat" length 3 < 5, no update      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Result: "apple" (length 5 > "bat" length 3)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Longest Word in Dictionary asks for the longest word from a list where every prefix of that word is also present in the list. This is a traversal application of the Trie pattern. After inserting all words and marking their end nodes, you traverse the trie from the root and only descend through nodes that are marked as complete words. If any intermediate prefix is missing, the DFS stops, correctly enforcing the one-character-at-a-time buildable rule.

The tie-break for lexicographic order comes free by iterating over children in sorted character order (index 0 to 25). Among words of equal length, the first one found in this sorted traversal is the lexicographically smallest. The update condition checks strictly greater length, so the first maximum-length word found is kept.

The time complexity is O(total characters) for trie construction and traversal, and the space is proportional to the total characters stored in the trie. An alternative approach sorts the words, then builds a set of buildable words by checking whether each word's prefix (minus the last character) is already in the set. This is simpler but requires sorting and uses a hash set.

At the National Bank of India, product feature codes are built incrementally, and a longer code is only valid if every shorter prefix is already registered. Rajesh used the trie approach to find the longest valid code chain, and the word-only descent rule naturally enforced the incremental-building constraint.

Remember one sentence: insert all words into a trie, then DFS only through nodes marked as complete words to find the longest path where every prefix is a valid word.
